dossier.mechanism: You play one of ten teahouse personalities (strength 400–1900), then Pikafish reads the whole game back on your own device: it grades every move on seven steps, names each mistake in xiangqi's own words (screenless cannon, trapped horse, broken advisors, a missed Iron Bolt) and turns those named mistakes into tomorrow's drills and mate problems. All of it happens on a board you can read without knowing Chinese, because a hybrid piece set puts each western symbol on its character.
dossier.audienceScene: Two visitors, both mostly on a phone after a search or an AI answer. (1) A western chess player who wants to try xiangqi but was put off by the characters on the pieces; they type 'learn xiangqi' or 'chinese chess app'. (2) A player who grew up with xiangqi or cờ tướng in a park, a family or the diaspora, and wants an engine to go through their own games offline, with no account; they type 'chinese chess offline' or 'pikafish iphone'. Desktop visitors coming from AI answers need the QR to get the app onto their iPhone.
dossier.culturalHome: Xiangqi's own culture: stone tables in parks, teahouses, Vietnamese sidewalk games, the big demonstration board in the commentary hall after a round, and the Ming and Qing manuals (Shiqing Yaqu 1570, Juzhongmi, the Plum Blossom manual). For the chess crossover, the culture of engine review. The bilingual (character + Latin) everyday world of Hong Kong, Taipei and Chinatowns. Chinese schooling: 田字格 character grids, red-pen marking and the 錯題本 mistake notebook.
dossier.mustProve: The first viewport has to show three things. First, one mistake named in xiangqi's own words, using the app's own string (e.g. 'Your horse stepped into the line and handed the enemy cannon the screen it needed.'), proof that the review explains rather than scores. Second, that the pieces are readable without Chinese (character + symbol + English name). Third, the offer: free, Premium from $1.99/mo, offline, no account, with the official badge and a desktop QR.
dossier.categoryDefault: The chess-app page: a dark navy ground, a 3D boxwood board with red and black discs, gold accents, an iPhone mockup on the right, 'Master Chinese Chess', and a grid of feature cards. The 'Chinese' version adds red and gold, lanterns, brush calligraphy and wood grain. The app's own UI (navy plus boxwood plus gold) already sits in this rut.
dossier.predictableOpposite: A white Swiss minimal page with a flat vector board, one red dot as the accent, and lots of air and tiny type. Calm, but it could sell any board game.
dossier.literalReading: The page as a xiangqi board: the river 楚河 漢界 across the middle, sections as ranks, discs as bullets. 'Full of xiangqi, move by move.' Only candidate 1 (the commentary board) uses the board, and it uses it as an instrument rather than as the page's map.

transparency.yml: 0 third-party SDKs, 0 tracking domains, no networking code, Data Not Collected, Pikafish GPL-3 compiled in, SwiftData with no CloudKit

Fonts checked on Fontsource (npm pack + fontTools): Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, Sofia Sans and Mona Sans lack ǎ ǐ ǒ ǔ (needed for the pinyin names); Source Sans 3, Fira Sans/Fira Sans Extra Condensed, Lexend, LXGW WenKai TC and Noto Sans/Serif TC have them. In the TC faces the ~60 needed CJK glyphs are spread across 14 slices (1.5–2.9 MB), so each style needs a one-time custom woff2 subset (~25–45 KB)

candidates.name: The commentary hall's big board (大盤講棋)
candidates.why: After a tournament round, and on decades of Chinese TV lectures, a master replays the game for the room on a giant vertical magnetic board and names each mistake. That is 'the engine reads it back to you, move by move.' It carries the mechanism directly: one pinned board replays a game while the app's own named-mistake strings hang beside it as the master's verdicts. This is the only candidate allowed the literal board.

candidates.name: Park stone tables (石桌棋盤)
candidates.why: The incised granite tables of Guangzhou parks, Hanoi sidewalks and Columbus Park in New York are the worldwide image of xiangqi, with regulars and kibitzers around them. It carries the ten personalities (a park grandmother who never leaves her palace) as a path of occupied tables, the next one sitting down once you beat the last twice. The review would be a kibitzer's verdict chalked on the stone.

candidates.name: The two-colour annotated manual (朱墨套印評點本)
candidates.why: 708 of the 902 mate problems come from eight Ming and Qing manuals. In the 評點 tradition a critic's verdicts are overprinted in vermilion over the black main text. It carries the mechanism as your game set as the main line, with Pikafish's grades and named mistakes as vermilion eyebrow notes (眉批). It sits on the cream + serif + red cluster and would need the hardest correction.

candidates.name: The pavement endgame stall (江湖殘局)
candidates.why: A cloth on the pavement, a famous classical ending (the Seven Stars, which the Advanced track teaches) and a card reading 'Red to move and win': this is the street's own mate problem. It carries the consecutive-check problems, and the app's honesty: book problems that don't hold up were left out, the opposite of a rigged stall. The hustle connotation fights the calm brand.

candidates.name: The mistake notebook, marked in red (錯題本 + 紅筆批改)
candidates.why: Anyone schooled in Chinese kept a 錯題本, copying out wrong answers to redo them. A teacher marked it in red pen: tick, circle, cross, a comment, a correction line. Characters were learned one at a time in 田字格 squares. It carries the whole loop literally: your mistake copied in, named, given one thing to do next game and dated for review (SM-2). A 田字格 row teaches the pieces the way the hybrid set does.

candidates.name: The tear-off almanac day (老黃曆 宜/忌)
candidates.why: The household almanac gives one thin sheet per day: a huge date numeral, a 宜 (do) list and a 忌 (avoid) list. It carries 'today's training from your weakest skill', with 宜 as the focus drill and 忌 as the mistake costing you most. But it holds only the daily-plan half of the loop, and it risks converging with the calendar worlds of Soon. or Taskful Day.

candidates.name: Bilingual metro wayfinding (character over English, line maps)
candidates.why: In the metros of Hong Kong, Taipei and Guangzhou the character name is set large over its English twin on enamel panels and tiled walls. That is how millions match characters to Latin at a glance, which is exactly the hybrid piece set. It carries every heading as a bilingual sign, the opponent ladder and your graded game as line maps, the drill modules already named like destinations (Mate Trail, Cannon Range, Palace Workshop), and the roadmap as dashed planned extensions.

type.display: Noto Sans TC 900 for the character line of every sign: 象棋 at 168px in the hero, section characters at 72–96px. It comes from a one-time ~60-glyph subset (the 14 piece characters including 傌 俥 炮 砲, 楚河漢界, 象棋, the section terms). Source Sans 3 700 sets the English line beneath: 64px in the hero, 40px on section signs.
type.text: Source Sans 3 400/600: panel copy at 19px/1.55, sign small print at 15px, the FAQ and fare table.
type.utility: Source Code Pro 500 for real data only: WXF/ICCS notation (C2=5, H2+3), move numbers on the game line, opponent strengths 400–1900.
type.rationale: Source Sans is the Latin half of Source Han Sans (= Noto Sans TC), so each bilingual sign is one superfamily, as a real sign system is. It sits in the humanist lineage of Chinese-metro English signage, and it carries the pinyin tone marks the opponents need (Xiǎobǎo, Nǎinai Chén), which Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Sofia Sans lack. Budget: SS3 latin 400/600/700 47 KB, plus a cut ~4 KB/weight pinyin-vowel file instead of full latin-ext, SCP 500 12 KB and the CJK subset ~30 KB, ≈ 100 KB in total.

styles.navigation: The white enamel line strip at the top is the microsite nav: the page's sections as stations on one black line, with scrollspy enlarging the current station dot. On mobile the 'Line' button opens a full-height vertical line map (links as stations, 48px targets) on enamel over the tile. Sub-pages show the same strip with their own station highlighted and a 'Xiangqiful' terminus linking home. Focus rings are a 3px sign-black ring with a 2px enamel offset.
styles.signatureInteraction: 'The line of your game'. An inline SVG route strip runs the full width: an illustrative 40-move game where each move is a station marker whose shape encodes the seven grades (best / great / good as filled dots of decreasing size, book a grey ring, inaccuracy a half-filled dot, mistake a ring with a bar, blunder a closed-station square, with a line key). Red's and Black's moves alternate above and below the line. The six key moments are interchange rings. Tapping or hovering one (a real <a href='#moment-n'>) slides its named-mistake sign under the strip with a small position diagram. On desktop a train marker travels the strip in step with scroll (CSS animation-timeline: view(), IntersectionObserver fallback). No-JS: the strip renders static and all six interchange signs are printed in order beneath it. Reduced motion: no train travel; signs swap without the slide.
styles.motionGrammar: Signage doesn't animate. Only things that move in a station move: the train marker along a line (linear, tied to scroll), the 'you are here' ring hopping between stations (120ms linear), and signs sliding 8px from their mounting edge with opacity (180ms ease-out). No parallax, no scale, no bounce, no hover lift. Under prefers-reduced-motion everything is static except focus rings.
styles.readModeVariant: Privacy, support and the five alternatives pages keep the tile ground and the line strip (with their own station lit). The reading column is one long enamel panel, 68ch, SS3 19px/1.6 in sign-black. H2s are bilingual signs where a true term exists (e.g. 私隱 / Privacy) and English-only otherwise; no invented Chinese. Privacy sections become notice panels with small data-flow pictograms (device → nothing leaves). Support is a 'Help point' panel with the email as the call button. Alternatives pages are an interchange board: 'Xiangqiful ↔ Xiangqi.com' as two connecting lines, the comparison as a connections table, the FAQ as enquiries, and an Exit panel to /apps/xiangqiful/.
styles.assetsNeeded: (1) A one-time Noto Sans TC 900 woff2 subset of ~60 glyphs (~30 KB, pyftsubset), named without any Reserved Font Name. (2) A cut pinyin-vowel file from SS3 latin-ext (ā á ǎ à ē é ě è ī í ǐ ì ō ó ǒ ò ū ú ǔ ù ü). (3) SVG exports of the app's seven western piece symbols from its asset catalog; do not redraw them. (4) A stroked pictogram set (exit, info, arrow, no-entry, interchange). (5) From the developer: an illustrative WXF game with Pikafish grades and the six FENs behind the example_insights; until then the strip is labelled 'illustrative'. (6) The full opponent list (10th name, strengths 6–9). Everything else runs on the existing icon, QR and screenshots.
styles.risk: The world is borrowed from public transport, not from xiangqi. If line metaphors leak into the copy it becomes a costume. Siblings are already using transit and wayfinding (allpaid's departures poster, earnlock's junction post), so this one must hold to its own devices: bilingual character-over-English signs, glazed tile, the game as a graded line. No yellow, no timetable grid. The drenched teal must stay ground, with all reading on enamel. Bilingual section terms must be checked against the app's zh-Hant localization.
styles.memoryTest: The xiangqi app whose page was a metro station: every heading was a Chinese character over its English name, my game was drawn as a line with the mistakes as interchanges, and a black Exit sign took me to the App Store.

styles.label: After-Round Big Board
styles.lineage: The tournament commentary board (大盤 / 掛盤講棋): a giant vertical white magnetic board on a stand, flat discs set on its intersections, slotted name plates above it, a flip move-counter, a ledge tray holding captured discs. A master replays the round for the hall with a pointer and blue dry-erase marker. Chinese TV xiangqi lectures used the same rig for decades.
styles.thesis: The page is the after-round lecture. One big lit board stays pinned in the hall and re-sets for each chapter while the commentary scrolls beside it, so the review mechanism is performed rather than described. It refuses the static hero screenshot and the wood-and-gold chess page.
styles.scene: A club player in the darkened commentary hall after the last round, on a folding chair, watching the master work the big magnetic board under a bank of stage lights; the board is the brightest thing in the room → dark ground, light board.

styles.signatureInteraction: 'The Lecture'. On desktop the board is position: sticky in the centre column while chapters scroll on the right and the record updates on the left. When a chapter crosses the reading line, its FEN (in a data attribute) re-sets the board. Discs lift (shadow 0→4px), slide straight along the grid with transforms (240ms, at most 3 discs per change) and seat; marker arrows draw via stroke-dashoffset (400ms); the flip counter turns. One IntersectionObserver, about 4 KB of JS. No-JS and mobile: every chapter carries its own server-rendered static SVG diagram above its text, and the sticky board is just chapter 1's diagram. Reduced motion: discs jump, marks appear whole, the counter changes without a flip.
styles.motionGrammar: Only what a commentator does moves: a disc lifts, slides and seats; a marker stroke draws at hand speed; a plate flips (160ms). Nothing else in the hall moves: no scroll reveals, no parallax, no hover lift on cards. With prefers-reduced-motion, state changes are instant.

styles.risk: Honest familiarity: this is my top-ranked direction because it is the most literal carrier. The board is the category's own object, so it sits closest to 'chess app shows a board'. Demonstration-board commentary is also shogi's 大盤解説 and a chess-tournament fixture, so it could converge with Shogiful or Chessful unless the white enamel, blue marker and Ming-bold discs stay specific. It is the most JS-dependent of the three, so the no-JS chapter diagrams must be first-class. Positions must come from the app, not be composed for the page.

styles.label: The Mistake Notebook
styles.lineage: The Chinese school exercise book: a stapled 練習本 on pale green 護眼 eye-care paper, a printed 方格 grid with 田字格 practice boxes for learning characters one at a time, and the 錯題本 (mistake notebook) every student keeps, copying each wrong answer to redo it. The teacher marks it in red ballpoint: tick, circle, cross, a wavy underline under the key line, a short comment and a 訂正 correction to rewrite.
styles.thesis: The page is your mistake notebook. Each entry is one mistake copied from a game, marked in red, explained, given one thing to do next game and dated for review, so Xiangqiful's loop (play → named mistake → tomorrow's training) is the page's structure. It refuses the feature-card grid and the dark 'engine analysis' dashboard.
styles.scene: A player at a desk by a daylit window with the exercise book open, a pencil, and the teacher's red pen beside it → light.

type.rationale: LXGW WenKai's Latin is drawn from Klee One's textbook hand, so one Kai face writes both the model characters a pupil copies and a teacher's neat red comments, and it covers the pinyin tone marks. Lexend was built from reading-proficiency research for learners, a fit for 'taught properly', and also covers pinyin. Neither is a serif display, which keeps paper + red out of the cream/serif cluster. Budget: WenKai latin 400/700 36 KB + Lexend latin 400/500 29 KB + cut pinyin-vowel files ~12 KB + Kai CJK subset ~45 KB ≈ 122 KB.

styles.signatureInteraction: 'Marking'. When each mistake entry reaches the reading line, the teacher's red pen marks it: the wrong move is struck through, the better square circled, the wavy underline runs under the key sentence and 'Review — due today' writes in. These are SVG stroke-dashoffset draws at hand speed (500–700ms, staggered 120ms). Each entry also has a 'Try the correction' <details> that reveals the better-move arrow on the pencil board (no JS needed). No-JS: every mark is present statically. Reduced motion: marks appear complete, with no drawing.
styles.motionGrammar: Only the pen moves: strokes draw once, in writing order, and never redraw on scroll-back. Paper, grid and type never move: no reveals, no parallax, no hover lift. <details> open without animated height. Under prefers-reduced-motion nothing draws.

styles.risk: Paper plus red pen sits nearest the cream + serif + red cluster. The pale green 護眼 paper, the Kai hand display and the Lexend body keep it out; it fails if the paper drifts warm or the display goes serif. A school notebook can read as child-facing or condescending to experienced diaspora players, so the teacher's voice must stay the app's adult copy, with no stickers, stars or grades. A sibling (Chessful's scoresheet, Shogiful's problem book) could also land on paper, so the 錯題本 and 田字格 specifics must lead. Keep red marks to a few per screen.
styles.memoryTest: It was an exercise book: my own mistake copied onto green squared paper, marked up in red pen, with the next thing to practise written underneath and a note that it was due for review today.

canon: Category standard played straight: dark navy page, a 3D boxwood board with red and black discs and gold accents in an iPhone frame beside 'Master Chinese Chess' and the badge, then a grid of feature cards and an FAQ. The owner's standing exit; not recommended.
notes: Degraded roll (roll service unreachable, no catalog challengers): seed 4b726ce3, assigned index 7, re-roll 1 = 5, so no further re-roll was needed. Mapping: A = candidate 7 (THE ROLL), B = candidate 1 (IMPECCABLE’S PICK, since neither N nor R1 is 1), C = candidate 5 (SECOND ROLL). The candidate order was fixed before the roll. Fonts were verified by npm pack + fontTools against Fontsource 5.3.0: all named faces exist with the weights given. Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, Sofia Sans and Mona Sans were rejected because they lack ǎ ǐ ǒ ǔ, which the opponents' pinyin names need. Every style needs a one-time CJK woff2 subset, because the Fontsource TC faces spread the ~60 needed glyphs across 14 slices totalling 1.5–2.9 MB; LXGW WenKai TC's chinese-traditional slice also lacks 傌 俥, which appear only in its numbered slices. Content gaps to fill from the app before building: FENs for the six example_insights moments (all three styles show a position beside a named mistake; until then the diagrams are labelled illustrative), the 10th opponent's name and strengths 6–9, and SVG exports of the western piece symbols. Piercing the Heart (screenshot 5) is the one real position on hand. No ratings, testimonials or user counts exist for this app, and none are shown. Sibling check: allpaid and earnlock already use transit and wayfinding worlds, so A drops exit-yellow and timetable grids and leans on bilingual signs, tile and the game-as-line.
